reviewedContributions.name: Personal & Professional Development

evidence.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
evidence.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
evidence.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
evidence.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design

reviewedContributions.finding: Required first-year academic development, research literacy and community collaboration; not target-generated elective.

reviewedContributions.name: Introduction to Economics

evidence.description2: Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.
evidence.profile: Introduces microeconomic principles and short-run macroeconomic analysis. The microeconomic component examines supply and demand, strategic interaction, consumer choice, production, costs and competitive markets. The macroeconomic component introduces output, unemployment and inflation, then relates goods and financial markets through the IS-LM model. Students use algebra and graphs to explain economic behaviour and apply models to economic issues.
evidence.topics: Supply and demand; Game theory; Rational consumer choice; Individual and market demand; Production and costs; Perfect competition; Aggregate output; Unemployment and inflation; Goods and financial markets; IS-LM model
evidence.methods: Algebraic and graphical economic analysis; Supply-and-demand analysis; Game-theoretic analysis; IS-LM modelling

reviewedContributions.finding: Scarcity, incentives, markets and choice introduce economic reasoning for land/water allocation; not a specialised rural-livelihoods course.

reviewedContributions.name: Microeconomics & Behavior

evidence.description2: Study how consumers and producers make decisions under scarcity. Explore key concepts such as rational choice, decision-making under uncertainty, and non-egoistic preferences. Analyze market structures, strategic interactions, and factor markets. Learn how markets function and examine the impact of regulation. Develop analytical tools to better understand behavior and engage with empirical research.
evidence.profile: Develops microeconomic theory through consumer behaviour, imperfectly competitive markets and economy-wide allocation. Students examine choice under uncertainty, non-egoistic preferences and cognitive limitations, then monopoly, strategic behaviour and labour and capital markets. General equilibrium, efficiency, externalities and government complete the analysis. Algebraic problem-solving and graphical analysis are connected to the interpretation and evaluation of research papers.
evidence.topics: Choice under uncertainty; Non-egoistic preferences; Cognitive limitations; Monopoly; Imperfect competition and strategic behaviour; Labour markets; Capital markets; General equilibrium; Market efficiency; Externalities; Government intervention
evidence.methods: Algebraic microeconomic analysis; Graphical economic analysis; Critical evaluation of economic research

reviewedContributions.finding: Microeconomicchoice/markets are substantive, but sustainablefarming/ecosystemprocesses andcommunity/governancebettercorrecttheclosesttargetweight. Economicfoundationsandallocationevidenceretainedelsewhere.

reviewedContributions.name: Public Economics

evidence.description2: Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.
evidence.profile: Examines government intervention through the efficiency and equity effects of public policy. Market failure, public goods and externalities provide foundations for studying public production, collective choice, spending and taxation. Health, education, welfare and social insurance illustrate expenditure and redistribution questions. Students apply economic models, interpret data and graphs, evaluate research and develop a research proposal and paper.
evidence.topics: Role and size of government; Market efficiency and failure; Public goods; Externalities; Efficiency and equity; Public production; Public choice; Public expenditure; Health and education policy; Welfare programs; Social insurance; Taxation and redistribution
evidence.methods: Economic model-based policy analysis; Efficiency and equity assessment; Interpretation of economic data and graphs; Critical evaluation of public-economics research

reviewedContributions.finding: Externalities, public goods, collective choice, efficiency/equity and expenditure analysis support evaluation of water/environmental policy; specific sector applications vary.

reviewedContributions.name: Econometrics

evidence.description2: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.

reviewedContributions.finding: Description-supported OLS/GLS/instrumental variables, causal/predictive inference and an empirical paper supply quantitative policy evidence; not GIS or hydrology.

reviewedContributions.name: Research Methods & Statistics

evidence.description2: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.
evidence.profile: Introduces empirical research design and statistical analysis, followed by a substantial student research project. Students study operationalization, measurement quality, sampling, surveys and experimental and nonexperimental designs, then descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression. R and R Commander support data display and analysis. Project teams develop instruments and a research plan, collect and analyze data, and report results under explicit research-ethics and privacy requirements.
evidence.topics: Scientific inquiry and hypotheses; Operationalization and measurement; Reliability and validity; Survey construction and sampling; Randomized and quasi-experimental designs; Nonexperimental and qualitative research; Descriptive statistics; Sampling distributions and estimation; Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals; Association and regression; Research ethics and anonymous data collection
evidence.methods: Survey design; Probability and nonprobability sampling; Experimental and nonexperimental research design; R and R Commander data analysis; Descriptive statistics and visualization; Scale-reliability analysis; One- and two-sample mean tests; ANOVA; Chi-square tests; Correlation and regression; Empirical data collection and analysis

reviewedContributions.finding: Research design, operationalisation, sampling, surveys/experiments, statistics and empirical reporting directly support human–environment investigation.

reviewedContributions.name: Introduction to Data Science

evidence.description2: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.
evidence.profile: Introduces data analysis and visualization in R through practical work with tabular, textual and spatial data. Students import, clean, transform and join data, explore patterns, and construct visualizations using tidy-data principles and the grammar of graphics. Web scraping and basic programming functions extend the workflow. A student research project applies these tools to a question using data from a field of interest.
evidence.topics: Data visualization; Exploratory data analysis; Tidy data; Data transformation and integration; Dates and times; Web data; Text data; Geospatial data; Programming functions; Data-based research questions
evidence.methods: R programming; ggplot visualization and grammar of graphics; Data cleaning, tidying and transformation; Data import and joins; Web scraping; Text-data analysis; Geospatial-data analysis

reviewedContributions.finding: R cleaning, transformation, visualisation and spatial/text data tools supply practical environmental-data preparation and inquiry.

reviewedContributions.name: Machine Learning

evidence.description2: Covers core machine learning techniques from linear regression to advanced tree‑based methods. Discusses strengths and weaknesses and applies methods to real data from fields like medicine, physics and economics.
evidence.profile: Introduces statistical learning for understanding data and predicting outcomes. Students study regression and classification, model accuracy, resampling, regularization, nonlinear models, trees, support vector machines and unsupervised learning. Practical assignments evaluate methods on real data using R or Python. Projects emphasize informative predictor construction, test-set prediction, appropriate model choice and clear reporting of results and limitations.
evidence.topics: Prediction and model accuracy; Regression and classification; Resampling and validation; Model selection and regularization; High-dimensional data; Nonlinear regression; Tree-based learning; Support vector methods; Dimension reduction; Unsupervised learning; Feature engineering
evidence.methods: Linear and logistic regression; Generative classification; Cross-validation and bootstrap; Subset selection; Ridge regression and LASSO; Splines and generalized additive models; Basic and advanced decision-tree methods; Support vector machines; Principal component analysis; Clustering; Predictive-performance evaluation; R or Python implementation

reviewedContributions.finding: Regression, model selection, validation, prediction and statistical learning extend environmental evidence analysis. No guaranteed remote-sensing project or specialist spatial algorithm is implied.

reviewedContributions.name: Mathematical Methods

evidence.description2: Introduces linear algebra (vectors, matrices, eigenvalues) and calculus (limits, differentiation, integration) to construct and solve equations. Provides problem‑solving skills applicable across disciplines.
evidence.profile: Develops single-variable calculus and related mathematical tools for modelling scientific problems. Functions, limits and differentiation lead to optimization, Taylor series, complex numbers, integration and differential equations. Students solve problems analytically and with Mathematica, including numerical approximation. A project implements, analyzes and adapts a dynamic model, requiring interpretation of its behaviour and explanation of the computational results.
evidence.topics: Functions and limits; Continuity; Differentiation; Optimization; Taylor series; Complex numbers; Definite and indefinite integrals; Integration techniques; First-order differential equations; Population-growth and predator–prey models; Second-order linear differential equations; Dynamic models
evidence.methods: Analytical differentiation and integration; Taylor approximation; Newton's method; Numerical integration; Euler's method; Analytical solution of differential equations; Computer algebra with Mathematica; Dynamic-model implementation and analysis

reviewedContributions.finding: Calculus, differential equations, dynamic models and numerical analysis support quantitative environmental investigation. Claims use the selected outline’s actual calculus scope rather than relying on the description’s broader linear-algebra wording.

reviewedContributions.name: Probability & Statistics

evidence.description2: Provides a foundation in mathematical statistics. Covers probability theory, discrete and continuous distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation; uses computer algebra software to develop theoretical understanding and practical skills.
evidence.profile: Provides a rigorous introduction to probability and mathematical statistics, from probability spaces and random variables to multivariate distributions and statistical inference. Students study estimation, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and maximum-likelihood methods, followed by an introduction to Bayesian reasoning. Mathematica simulations verify analytical results. A substantial project implements and compares random-sampling algorithms, including inverse sampling, accept-reject sampling and Gibbs sampling.
evidence.topics: Probability spaces and conditional probability; Random variables and expectation; Moment-generating functions; Discrete and continuous distributions; Multivariate and conditional distributions; Transformations and correlation; Sampling and order statistics; Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests; Estimation efficiency; Bayesian inference; Monte Carlo methods
evidence.methods: Analytical probability calculation; Maximum-likelihood estimation and testing; Chi-square tests; Bootstrap; EM algorithm; Bayesian updating; Inverse-transform sampling; Accept-reject sampling; Gibbs sampling; Monte Carlo simulation in Mathematica

reviewedContributions.finding: Probability, distributions, estimation, tests, uncertainty and simulation directly strengthen rigorous environmental-data reasoning; its theoretical emphasis differs from applied survey statistics.

reviewedContributions.name: Building with Nature

evidence.description2: Introduces the sustainable engineering approach of working with natural processes for flood protection, land reclamation and port development. Covers history and principles of ecosystem‑based design, explores case studies and includes guest lectures and field excursions.
evidence.profile: Introduces approaches that combine human infrastructure with natural processes and ecosystem health, with particular attention to Zeeland and the history of water management on Walcheren. Students examine applications across sandy and muddy coasts, lowland lakes, rivers and estuaries, cities and ports. Projects investigate ecological connectivity and formulate a Building with Nature intervention; a practical wall-building project explores constructed structures.
evidence.topics: Nature-based infrastructure; Coastal and water management; Walcheren's water-management history; Sandy and muddy coasts; Lowland lakes; Rivers and estuaries; Urban nature-based solutions; Harbour habitats; Habitat connectivity; Ecoducts and fish ladders
evidence.methods: Building with Nature case analysis; Ecological-corridor project analysis; Nature-based intervention design; Construction and testing of model walls

reviewedContributions.finding: Nature-based flood protection, water infrastructure and an intervention-design project directly supply applied land/water design principles, without irrigation or canal-calculation equivalence.

reviewedContributions.name: Living with Water

evidence.description2: Explores sustainable water management in delta regions. Focuses on adaptation to rising seas, floods and land subsidence; engages students in projects in Zeeland; and highlights nature‑based solutions and resilient infrastructure.
evidence.profile: Examines how delta societies manage water risks and opportunities, using Zeeland as a central case. Physical and ecological challenges such as flooding, salinization, freshwater scarcity, subsidence and pollution are connected to infrastructure, history, governance, law and justice. Students evaluate engineered and nature-based responses, considering trade-offs and long-term consequences. Site-based inquiry and a project apply these concepts to context-sensitive adaptation in a delta region.
evidence.topics: Delta environments; Flood risk and protection; Drainage and freshwater management; Sea-level rise and subsidence; Salinization; Water infrastructure and ecological consequences; Water governance, law and justice; Contaminants and pollution; EU Water Framework Directive; Nature-based adaptation; Urban ecology and water; Long-term delta resilience
evidence.methods: Site-based water-management case analysis; Comparative appraisal of engineered and nature-based solutions; Context-sensitive adaptation-strategy development

reviewedContributions.finding: Flooding, freshwater scarcity, drainage, salinisation, subsidence and engineered/nature-based adaptation directly sustain water management in delta landscapes.

reviewedContributions.name: R3: Recycling, Recovery, Remediation

evidence.description2: Examines strategies and technologies towards a circular economy. Explores resource security and stewardship, develops lab skills and inorganic chemistry knowledge, and connects to themes at the Delta Climate Center.
evidence.profile: Studies resource circularity through solar-panel recycling, metal recovery from electronic waste, and soil remediation using plants and mycelium. Theory and extensive laboratory work connect material composition and separation technologies to resource yields, environmental consequences and recycling constraints. Students develop leaching protocols, analyze metal concentrations and recovery, cultivate fungal networks, and use microscopy to characterize materials and mycelium growth.
evidence.topics: Circular resource supply; Solar-cell and solar-panel recycling; Delamination and material separation; Electronic waste; Pyrometallurgy and hydrometallurgy; Precious-metal recovery; Plastic-recycling legislation; Phytoremediation; Mycoremediation; Mycelium-based soil amendments
evidence.methods: Solar-panel dismantling and physical separation; Chemical leaching; Experimental-protocol design; ICP metal analysis; Electrochemical recovery; Scanning electron microscopy and EDS; Mycelium cultivation and growth characterization; Recovery-yield and resource-potential calculations

reviewedContributions.finding: Resource recovery, material stewardship, laboratory analysis and plant/mycelial soil remediation complement land/resource management; metal recycling is not erosion-control engineering.

reviewedContributions.name: Governance of Sustainability

evidence.description2: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
evidence.profile: Analyzes sustainability as a problem of collective decision-making involving governments, markets and civil society. Concepts of institutions, power, participation, justice and problem complexity frame competing technological and systemic responses. Structured cases examine food, freshwater, energy and climate mitigation. Students apply governance frameworks to a Zeeland issue, consult relevant organizations or experts, and produce policy advice or an evaluation assessing effectiveness, feasibility and stakeholder interests.
evidence.topics: Institutions, actors and power; Collective action and common-pool resources; Governance modes and networks; Techno-optimism and ecological limits; Climate justice; Populism and environmental politics; Wicked and long-term problems; Public participation; Food, water and energy governance; Markets, public goods and externalities; Adaptive and global governance; Climate mitigation; Policy effectiveness and feasibility
evidence.methods: Governance-framework application; Problem diagnosis and causal analysis; Stakeholder and policy-option matrices; Policy evaluation; Policy-advice memo development; Stakeholder and expert interviewing; Comparative analysis of normative policy perspectives

reviewedContributions.finding: Actors, institutions, power, participation and collective decisions in food/water/climate, with policy advice and stakeholder inquiry, directly support land-water governance.

reviewedContributions.name: Introduction to Biodiversity

evidence.description2: The biosphere consists of millions of living species. In this course we will travel through the tree of life, starting with bacteria and single-celled eukaryotes such as reef-building dinoflagellates and disease-causing apicomplexans. Next, we will look at the multicellular groups: plants, seaweeds, fungi and animals. We will also investigate the relevance of biodiversity for human society in fields such as food and food security, economy, climate and health.
evidence.profile: Surveys the diversity and evolutionary relationships of living organisms across the tree of life. Students examine prokaryotes, protists, fungi, plants and animals, their distinguishing characteristics and ecological roles. Practical work introduces microscopy, organism identification and biodiversity measurement. A small project investigates a selected phylogenetic branch, supported by literature searching, data collection and analysis.
evidence.topics: Biodiversity and its measurement; Phylogenetic relationships; Viruses; Bacteria and archaea; Protists; Fungi; Plant diversity; Invertebrates; Vertebrates and primates; Evolutionary history; Organismal ecological roles
evidence.methods: Microscopy; Organism identification using identification apps; Rank-abundance diagrams; Species-saturation curves; Biodiversity indices; Phylogenetic research; Scholarly database searching; Biodiversity data collection and analysis

reviewedContributions.finding: Biodiversity and organismal ecological roles provide a specific biological foundation for environmental impacts and ecosystem resilience; not the complete general ecology course.

reviewedContributions.name: Ecosystems Uncovered: How Nature Works

evidence.description2: Focuses on basic principles of ecology. Studies how environmental conditions affect organisms and examines ecological principles governing individuals, populations, communities and ecosystems, including ecological modelling and applied case studies.
evidence.profile: Develops ecological principles from organisms and populations to communities and ecosystems. Environmental conditions, resources and life cycles frame competition, feeding relationships, selection, population dynamics and biodiversity. Energy and matter cycles connect ecological processes to conservation and human impacts. Dedicated practical sessions teach simple ecological modelling in R, and a small research project communicates findings through a poster.
evidence.topics: Ecology and evolution; Environmental conditions and resources; Climate and life cycles; Ecological niches; Competition and cohabitation; Predation and food webs; Natural selection; Population dynamics; Biodiversity patterns; Ecological succession; Ecosystem energy and matter fluxes; Global cycles; Conservation and human impacts; Ecosystem value
evidence.methods: Ecological modelling in R; Population-dynamics calculations; Ecosystem energy and matter-flux calculations; Ecological research-project design and analysis

reviewedContributions.finding: Population/community/ecosystem processes, resource conditions, cycles and R ecological modelling directly support land use, agroecosystems and environmental management.

reviewedContributions.name: Sustainable Farming & Innovation

evidence.description2: Discusses environmental impacts of agriculture and explores sustainable agriculture approaches such as agroecology, organic farming, conservation agriculture, precision agriculture, sustainable livestock farming, agroforestry, permaculture, crop rotation, integrated pest management and sustainable supply chains.
evidence.profile: Examines how food production can balance human needs with environmental impacts. Students assess current agriculture, horticulture and animal husbandry, their effects on biodiversity and ecosystems, and alternative practices and innovations. Aquaculture, alternative animal-protein sources and farming for other industries extend the comparison. A literature-based project critically investigates a chosen sustainable-farming question and reports the evidence without prescribing a single preferred approach.
evidence.topics: Agricultural and horticultural systems; Environmental impacts of farming; Wildlife and biodiversity; Modification of current farming practices; Alternative agricultural approaches; Animal husbandry; Aquaculture; Alternative protein sources; Farming for non-food industries; Sustainable-farming innovation
evidence.methods: Scientific-literature review; Comparative appraisal of farming practices and innovations

reviewedContributions.finding: Farming practices, agroecosystem impacts, alternative production and literature-based comparison directly strengthen the target’s agricultural and land-management core, without claiming crop-physiology/yield modelling equivalence.

reviewedContributions.name: Dynamic Earth

evidence.description2: Introduces Earth Science by focusing on interactions among the deep earth, lithosphere and hydrosphere. Highlights key cycles shaping Earth’s surface and includes indoor/outdoor labs and a multi‑day field excursion.
evidence.profile: Introduces Earth science by linking surface geology to deep-Earth and geophysical processes. Students study rocks, minerals, sedimentation, deformation, stratigraphy, plate tectonics, seismology, the mantle and core, and interactions with climate and other Earth systems. Field and practical work teaches observation and measurement, rock and mineral identification, and reconstruction of geological history. An Ardennes field investigation produces a geological cross-section, stratigraphic column and interpretive report.
evidence.topics: Plate tectonics and the Wilson cycle; Minerals and rock formation; Volcanism and metamorphism; Sedimentation and facies; Structural deformation; Stratigraphy and palaeontology; Seismology and seismic waves; Geomagnetism and gravity; Mantle and core processes; Earth-system and climate interactions; Geological history; Geohazards
evidence.methods: Geological field observation and measurement; Rock and mineral identification; Geological mapping and profiling; Stratigraphic-column construction; Geological cross-section construction; Sediment and facies interpretation; Geological-history reconstruction

reviewedContributions.finding: Rocks, minerals, sedimentation, geological mapping and field measurement provide physical-landscape foundations; not a direct soil-classification course.

reviewedContributions.name: Natural Hazards, Risks & Adaptations

evidence.description2: Covers geoscience principles and analytical tools to understand natural disasters. Compares risks from climate change‑driven events and mining disasters and teaches actions to reduce risks from events like earthquakes, droughts and toxic algae blooms.

reviewedContributions.finding: The official description supports drought and other geohazards, risk analysis and adaptation. Full consideration without inventing unlisted hydrological modelling or field techniques.

reviewedContributions.name: Earth Observation

evidence.description2: Provides hands‑on experience with GIS and data integration using geospatial data from satellites and drones. Uncovers how human actions impact ecosystems and climate and promotes sustainable practices through research projects.
evidence.profile: Develops geospatial analysis for investigating environmental change and designing responses to Earth-system problems. Hands-on ArcGIS Pro work covers spatial data models, georeferencing, projections, visualization, queries, transformations and surface analysis. Remote-sensing foundations extend into spectral signatures, acquisition systems, preprocessing and image processing. A collaborative case study applies geospatial methods to an environmental research question.
evidence.topics: Spatial concepts and data models; Geospatial databases; Georeferencing and map projections; Spatial visualization; Spatial queries and transformations; Surface analysis; Earth-observation tools; Spectral signatures; Remote-sensing acquisition systems; Image preprocessing and processing; Environmental geospatial applications
evidence.methods: ArcGIS Pro spatial analysis; Spatial-data collection and database management; Georeferencing and coordinate transformation; Geospatial visualization and queries; Surface analysis; Remote-sensing preprocessing; Image processing; Geospatial case-study design

reviewedContributions.finding: ArcGIS Pro, georeferencing, spatial databases, surface analysis and remote-sensing/image methods directly support geospatial land-water investigation.

reviewedContributions.name: Soils & Aquifers

evidence.description2: Explores soils and aquifers through fieldwork and lab analyses. Covers soil formation, properties, health and remediation and investigates mapping aquifers for geothermal energy, coastal defence and freshwater resource assessment.
evidence.profile: Examines soils and shallow aquifers through soil science, environmental chemistry and applied geophysics. Soil formation, functions, quality and threats connect to texture, structure, composition, biological activity and salinization. Field sampling and laboratory investigations characterize soil properties and sediment-cell behaviour. Seismic, electrical-resistivity and electromagnetic surveys investigate physical and geophysical properties of soils and aquifers. Students document procedures and observations, process field data in Excel, interpret results and develop evidence-based field and laboratory reports.
evidence.topics: Soil formation, functions and taxonomy; Soil quality, amendments and threats; Soil texture, structure and aggregate stability; Soil moisture and organic matter; Soil chemistry, pH and metals; Soil biology; Sediment-cell behaviour; Shallow aquifers, salinization and freshwater interventions; Physical and geophysical properties of soils and aquifers; Seismology; Electrical resistivity; Electromagnetic surveying
evidence.methods: Soil coring and field sampling; Visual soil-structure assessment (grass-VESS); Aggregate-stability, texture and sieve tests; Soil pH, moisture, organic-content and leaching analyses; Microscopy and SEM-EDS; Sample preparation for ICP/IC and interpretation of ICP results; Methylene-blue testing with spectrophotometry/titration; Seismic surveying; Electrical-resistivity and electromagnetic surveying; Field-data processing in Excel

reviewedContributions.finding: Soil formation, structure/quality, moisture, aquifers, sampling, chemical tests and geophysical surveying directly address soil/water processes and field evidence.

reviewedContributions.name: Earth System Science Tools

evidence.description2: Explores interactions among biosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere and atmosphere. Teaches system modelling, uses proxies and isotope tracers to study past and future climates and includes a field trip focused on greenhouse gas pathways.

reviewedContributions.finding: Description-supported Earth-system interactions, system modelling, proxies and isotope tracers, and greenhouse-gas field inquiry deepen environmental and climate analysis; not a substitute for GIS.

reviewedContributions.name: Environmental Biogeochemistry

evidence.description2: Investigates natural waters and their interactions with rocks, soils and minerals. Examines biogeochemical processes and cycles, including weathering, mineral formation, absorption, water treatment and resource recovery; utilises geochemical modelling and a case study.
evidence.profile: Examines chemical and biological controls on near-surface Earth systems, especially interactions among water, minerals, rocks and soils. Students study aqueous composition, equilibrium, speciation, carbonate and redox chemistry, adsorption, weathering and biomineralization. Laboratory investigations and geochemical modelling connect these processes to contaminant behaviour, wastewater treatment, remediation and resource recovery. A project applies geochemical principles to a current environmental issue.
evidence.topics: Natural-water composition; Chemical equilibrium and ionic activity; Aqueous speciation and complexation; Mineral saturation, precipitation and dissolution; Carbonate equilibria, alkalinity and buffering; Ocean acidification; Redox processes and microbial controls; Adsorption and mineral surfaces; Weathering and clay formation; Biomineralization; Contaminant transport; Environmental remediation and resource recovery
evidence.methods: Geochemical equilibrium and speciation modelling; Geochemist's Workbench; Piper diagrams; Pourbaix and stability diagrams; Laboratory geochemical investigations; Geochemical data interpretation

reviewedContributions.finding: Water–soil–mineral interactions, equilibrium, redox, adsorption, weathering and geochemical modelling directly deepen soil and water process understanding and contamination/remediation evidence.

reviewedContributions.name: Earth's Resources

evidence.description2: Provides in‑depth geoscience research into resource and environmental challenges such as nuclear waste storage, geothermal energy and CO₂ capture. Students conduct literature reviews and produce class reports for presentation to a professional conference.

reviewedContributions.finding: Description-supported geoscientific inquiry into geothermal resources, waste storage and carbon capture, literature reviews and professional-conference reporting develop resource evaluation; no unlisted groundwater engineering is assumed.

reviewedContributions.name: Sustainability Essentials I

evidence.description2: Provides key concepts in physics, chemistry, materials science, mathematics and modelling necessary for sustainability. Uses a case study to connect concepts to real‑world sustainability challenges and prepares students for 200‑level sustainability courses.
evidence.profile: Uses planetary boundaries to introduce scientific tools for understanding sustainability and human impacts on Earth systems. Students interpret graphs and uncertainty, build simple dynamic models, and learn chemical, thermodynamic and mechanical principles relevant to environmental processes. Topics connect climate, ocean acidification, nutrient cycles, energy and materials. An iterative laboratory project makes starch-based biopolymers and measures their strength and elasticity to improve the formulation.
evidence.topics: Planetary boundaries and the Anthropocene; Exponential growth and environmental change; Graphs, rates and uncertainty; Dynamic systems; Chemical bonds, reactions and equilibria; Ocean acidification and nutrient cycles; Thermodynamics and entropy; Greenhouse gases and energy; Ozone depletion; Newtonian mechanics, stress and strain; Biopolymers and material properties
evidence.methods: Graph interpretation and comparison; Fermi estimation; Difference-equation and first-order linear differential-equation modelling; Elementary differentiation and integration; Biopolymer preparation; Strength and elasticity measurement; Iterative experimental improvement

reviewedContributions.finding: Chemical, physical, mathematical and dynamic-modelling foundations support later soil, water, materials and environmental analysis; it is not a full hydraulics course.

reviewedContributions.name: Sustainability Essentials II

evidence.description2: Builds on Sustainability Essentials I. Applies tools and knowledge to a real‑world sustainability case study and allows students to delve deeper into aspects connected to their field of interest.
evidence.profile: Connects wave physics, chemistry and materials science to sustainability questions. Students study wave behaviour and observation methods, chemical analysis, microscopic material structure and macroscopic stress and strain. Practical sessions include wave applications and chemistry laboratory work. Reflective inquiries and a final project critically assess sustainability campaigns, identify greenwashing and communicate evidence-based improvements to a public audience.
evidence.topics: Electromagnetic and mechanical waves; Wave composition and interference; Optical spectroscopy; Electron microscopy; Inorganic and organic chemistry; Chemical testing; Material structure and crystallography; Stress and strain; Sustainable material design; Geological wave applications; Nuclear power and waste; Greenwashing
evidence.methods: Oscilloscope wave visualization; Optical-spectroscopy interpretation; Fourier wave analysis; Copper dissolution and chemical analysis; Laboratory logbook documentation; Stress-strain analysis; Mohr's-circle application; Evidence-based greenwashing case analysis; Public sustainability-communication design

reviewedContributions.finding: Wave, chemical-analysis, material/stress tools and laboratory practice support the selected geoscience/remediation sequence; critical sustainability communication complements the applied concept.

reviewedContributions.name: Climate Change

evidence.description2: Focuses on drivers and impacts of anthropogenic climate change on sea level, ocean acidification, ecology and society. Discusses adaptation and mitigation solutions, including renewable energy systems, carbon storage and climate‑adaptive planning, and examines climate governance and justice.
evidence.profile: Introduces climate-change science, societal impacts, and mitigation and adaptation. Students examine greenhouse gases, feedbacks, tipping points, ocean acidification and sea-level rise, then consequences for ecosystems, agriculture, transport, buildings and health. Climate justice, governance, communication and misinformation connect physical changes to social responses. Solution pathways include energy systems, carbon removal and climate-adaptive planning. Students interview a stakeholder and produce a short film, alongside reflection on their own role.
evidence.topics: Anthropogenic climate change; Greenhouse gases; Feedback loops and tipping points; Ocean acidification and sea-level rise; Biosphere impacts; Agriculture, transport and construction; Climate and health; Climate justice and governance; Paris Agreement; Renewable energy and sustainable heat; Carbon removal and geoengineering; Climate communication and misinformation; Climate anxiety; Mitigation and adaptation
evidence.methods: Stakeholder interviewing; Short-film production for climate communication; Source-credibility evaluation; What? So What? Now What? reflective model

reviewedContributions.finding: Climate processes, sea-level change, agriculture, adaptation, governance and justice directly support land-water climate questions.

reviewedContributions.name: Renewable System Design

evidence.description2: Teaches assessment of energy usage patterns and strategies for reducing consumption or transitioning to cleaner energy. Explores solar, wind and bioenergy solutions and includes technical and economic analysis; students deliver a report and presentation to a partner company.

reviewedContributions.finding: Solar/wind/bioenergyassessmentandpartnerreportarevalidtechnicalappliedstudy;statisticaluncertaintyandmodellingmoremateriallyimplementwater/climateenvironmentalevidencethanrenewable-energy-systemdesign.

reviewedContributions.name: Research in a Sustainable Delta

evidence.description2: In this project course you will work in small teams of two or three students on a research problem relevant for sustainability in the broadest sense. We are looking for collaborations with local companies and other institutions. The research questions are supplied by a regional institution or company that is active in areas related to sustainability in the broadest sense. In this way it is guaranteed that the research projects are indeed relevant for the Zeeland delta. Furthermore, students will have access to expertise and/or facilities of the external partner, which will broaden their perspective.
